title: Giving an opinion
goal: Make the opinion sound considered, and the reason precise.
base: My opinion is that this solution is good because it has many advantages.

steps.text: I believe this solution is particularly effective, largely because it offers several tangible benefits.
steps.why: Stronger verbs (offers) and precise adjectives (tangible) do the work that “good” and “many” couldn't. “Largely” shows you've weighed other factors.

steps.text: I would argue that this solution is particularly compelling, given the range of advantages it offers.
moves: “I would argue that”: positions you in a debate
end-weight: the reason closes the sentence
steps.why: “I would argue” signals an arguable claim, which sounds more intellectually honest than “I believe”. “Given + noun phrase” packs the reason into a phrase instead of a whole clause.

alternatives.text: To my mind, this is by far the strongest option on the table.
There is a strong case for adopting this solution.
Honestly, I think this is our best bet.

title: Describing a problem
goal: Replace vague size words and make the consequence explicit.
base: There is a big problem with the app because a lot of users can't log in.

steps.text: We are facing a significant issue with the app, as a large number of users are unable to log in.
moves: “there is a big problem” → “we are facing a significant issue”
steps.why: An active verb (facing) and a measured adjective (significant) sound more professional than “big”. “Issue” is the standard professional softener.

steps.text: A login failure affecting a substantial proportion of our users is currently our most pressing concern.
moves: nominalisation: “users can't log in” → “a login failure”
steps.why: The whole problem becomes a single noun phrase subject, which lets you add a judgement at the end (most pressing concern). This is the backbone of formal reporting.

alternatives.text: Loads of people can't log in, so that's the big one right now.
We've identified a login issue affecting a number of users and are working on a fix.

title: Contrasting two ideas
goal: Link the two ideas with a single, well-built sentence.
base: Online courses are cheap. But they are not very good for motivation.

steps.text: While online courses are relatively inexpensive, they tend to do little to sustain students' motivation.
moves: “not very good for” → “do little to sustain”
steps.why: “Cheap” can imply poor quality: “inexpensive” is neutral. “Do little to + verb” is an elegant, natural negative.

steps.text: Whatever online courses gain in affordability, they often lose in their capacity to keep students motivated.
moves: parallel structure: gain in X / lose in Y
steps.why: Parallelism makes the contrast feel inevitable. It's memorable and persuasive, but use it once per text, not in every paragraph.

alternatives.text: Online courses may be affordable, but motivation is another matter.
Admittedly, online courses are affordable; however, they struggle to keep learners engaged.

title: Saying something is important
base: It is very important to protect personal data.

steps.why: Shorter and stronger. Gradable adjectives with “very” are often a sign of a missing precise word (very important → essential, crucial, vital).

steps.text: The protection of personal data is not merely desirable but a fundamental prerequisite for public trust.
moves: specifying WHY it matters: “for public trust”
steps.why: C2 writing doesn't just say something is important: it says for what, and how much. The “not merely… but” pattern escalates the claim.

alternatives.text: Personal data must be protected at all costs.

title: Expressing a result
goal: Replace “so” and make the causal chain elegant.
base: We changed the algorithm, so the app is faster now.

steps.text: Following changes to the algorithm, the app now runs significantly faster.
steps.why: “Following” moves the cause into a phrase and lets the result take the main clause, where the reader's attention is.

steps.text: A redesign of the core algorithm has substantially reduced load times, thereby improving the overall user experience.
steps.why: “Thereby” chains a consequence of the consequence without starting a new sentence. It's formal: avoid it in speech.

alternatives.text: We reworked the algorithm and the app's noticeably quicker now.
As a result of the algorithm changes, performance has improved considerably.

title: Disagreeing politely
base: You are wrong, this plan will not work.

steps.text: I see where you're coming from, but I'm not convinced this plan will work.
moves: acknowledge first: “I see where you're coming from”
“you are wrong” → “I'm not convinced” (shift the focus to yourself)
steps.why: In English, disagreement is framed as your perception, not the other person's failure. This keeps the discussion on the idea.

steps.text: I take your point, but I have some reservations about whether the plan is workable in its current form.
moves: “I have some reservations”: diplomatic, still clear
“in its current form”: leaves room for improvement
steps.why: “In its current form” turns a rejection into an invitation to revise it. Diplomacy is precision about what exactly you disagree with.

alternatives.text: I'm not sure that's going to fly, to be honest.
alternatives.when: Casual, with a colleague you know well.

alternatives.text: With respect, I'd question some of the assumptions behind this plan.
alternatives.when: Formal meeting; note that “with respect” signals firm disagreement.

title: Describing a trend
goal: Describe change with precise verbs and adverbs.
base: The number of users went up a lot last year.

steps.text: The number of users rose sharply last year.
steps.why: Trend verbs + adverbs: rose sharply / steadily / marginally; fell dramatically / slightly. They describe both direction and speed.

steps.text: Last year saw a threefold increase in the number of users, far outpacing initial projections.
moves: comparison with expectations: “far outpacing initial projections”
steps.why: “[Time period] saw + noun” is a typical report structure. Adding a reference point (projections) gives the number meaning.

alternatives.when: Concise and powerful: often the best choice.

title: Concluding
goal: Avoid “In conclusion, I think…” and end with a real synthesis.
base: In conclusion, I think social media has good and bad sides.

steps.text: Ultimately, social media is neither inherently good nor bad; its impact depends largely on how it is used.
moves: “its impact depends on…”: a real claim
steps.why: A good conclusion doesn't restate that there are two sides: it says what decides between them.

steps.text: The question, then, is not whether social media is harmful, but under what conditions it becomes so, and who should be responsible for setting them.
moves: reframing: “The question, then, is not… but…”
steps.why: Reframing the question is the hallmark of a mature conclusion: it shows you've understood what the debate is really about.

alternatives.text: On balance, the benefits seem to outweigh the drawbacks, provided that…
alternatives.when: When you want to take a side, with a condition.
